v.why: Adding a 3x3 conv on the direct input-to-output edge creates a new path, which helps much more than swapping out an existing op (exps 1-7 vs 8-10).
With edge 4 absent, node 3 has few or no inputs, so a conv on edge 3 restores a critical path (exps 3-5 give +12 to +53 on CIFAR-10 vs +9 to +14 in exps 1-2).
Replacing the direct skip connection loses the residual path; exp 9 is negative on all three datasets.
Adding a residual shortcut where none existed gives large gains (+15 to +35) across all datasets, larger than replacing a conv or pool (exps 36-37).
In pooling-dominated cells there is no learned feature to pass along the shortcut, so the skip barely helps (exp 35: about +1-2).
Removing edge 3 when edge 4 is also gone leaves node 3 with only one or no inputs, which is catastrophic (exp 72: -53 on CIFAR-10; exp 74: -26 on CIFAR-100).
Removing edge 4 when edge 3 is already absent cuts the remaining paths into the output (exp 44: -42 on CIFAR-10).
When the direct edge 3 is missing, a conv on edge 4 restores an input path to the output (exp 93: +42/+18/+5).
Adding the node 2-to-output conv helps greatly when edge 3 is absent (exp 17: +38) but is often negative when edges 3 and 4 already feed the output (exps 11-14).

Making edge 1 a pooling op is tolerated when other edges carry 3x3 convs (exps 51-53, 56-58, 60 are mixed) but hurts on every dataset in skip, 1x1 or pool cells, where edge 1 held the only 3x3 conv (exps 54, 55, 59).

When the parent keeps several paths into node 3, the same edit does much less.
